creator: Chris Huber Reitz
name: Stack Overflow — Generative AI content policy (Help Center)
quote: Generative artificial intelligence (a.k.a. GPT, LLM, generative AI, genAI) tools may not be used to generate content for Stack Overflow.
quote_label: Stack Overflow Help Center, 'What is this site’s policy on content generated by generative artificial intelligence tools?' (read live 2026-10-11)

provenance.note: Disconfirmation probe (reserve-where-proof-is-cheap; sibling of QEMU). D1=1: content 'must either be your own original work, or your summary of the properly referenced work of others'; no audit trail. D2=2: 'Users who ask questions on Stack Overflow expect to receive an answer authored and vetted by a human.' D3=0: no labeling route — a ban, and citing the tool does not cure it ('even if someone explicitly cites the generative artificial intelligence tool as an author in their content'). D4=1: names fabrication as a reason ('may fabricate false or misleading information'; cited sources 'may not exist at all') but no synthetic-identity provision. D5=2: human authoring and vetting is the condition of posting. D6=2: 'the person who asked a question needs a correct answer'. Enforcement: deletion with reputation, warning, suspension. c2_fit=partially: code answers are cheap to check in principle, yet reserved. The stated reasons are not code correctness: they are sourcing ('not capable of citing the sources of knowledge used up to the standards of the Stack Exchange network') and the asker's own inability to vet. The QEMU split recurs in a new form — the scarce proof is provenance and vetting capacity, not whether the code runs. c3=Evidential: the human-authorship expectation is justified on factual grounds ('This ensures that the answer is factual, relevant, and complete').
